name: Inter-VLAN Routing
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Route between VLANs with router-on-a-stick, Layer 3 switch SVIs, routed ports and Layer 3 EtherChannels, and troubleshoot each.

lesson.intro: VLANs split a network into separate subnets, so something must route between them. Build router on a stick, Layer 3 switch SVIs, routed ports and Layer 3 EtherChannels, follow a packet through each, and fix the faults that break them.
objectives: Configure router on a stick with 802.1Q subinterfaces, including the native VLAN
Configure a Layer 3 switch with ip routing and SVIs, and trace a packet through it
Choose between an SVI, a routed port and a Layer 3 EtherChannel
Troubleshoot wrong dot1q tags, missing ip routing, down SVIs and missing return routes

sections.title: Why VLANs need a router
sections.key: Each VLAN is its own subnet, so hosts send off-subnet traffic to a default gateway that a router subinterface, an SVI or a routed interface must own.
sections.body:
PC-A (VLAN 10) pings PC-B (VLAN 20). They share a switch, a meter apart, and the ping fails.

That is VLANs doing their job. A Layer 2 switch forwards frames only within a VLAN, and each VLAN is its own subnet. PC-A sends the packet to its **default gateway**, 192.168.10.1, in a frame addressed to the gateway's MAC. If nothing owns that address, PC-A's ARP for it goes unanswered.

[[visual]]

So some Layer 3 device needs an address in every VLAN, and it routes between those connected subnets like any router:

[[visual 2]]

Whatever the design, hosts see the same thing: a gateway in their own subnet whose MAC they learn with ARP.

visual.title: Four places the gateway can live
rows: One physical router interface and access link per VLAN
Two or three VLANs; burns a port per VLAN
`interface vlan N` on a Layer 3 switch
Campus user VLANs, routed in hardware
A Layer 3 switch port with `no switchport` and an IP address

sections.tip: One VLAN, one subnet, one gateway address. When those line up, inter-VLAN routing is ordinary routing between connected subnets.
sections.pitfall: Putting hosts from different VLANs in the same subnet. They still cannot talk (ARP stays inside each VLAN), and routing cannot fix it because the addressing claims they are local.

activity.title: VLANs isolate, trunks extend
activity.prompt: Put two hosts on the same switch in different VLANs and test reachability: notice they cannot talk even though they share a switch. Then make same-VLAN hosts on both switches reach each other across the trunk. That trunk is the Layer 2 half of router-on-a-stick.

check.question: PC-A (VLAN 10) and PC-B (VLAN 20) connect to SW1, a Layer 2 switch with no router attached. What happens when PC-A pings PC-B?
choices: It works because both ports are on the same switch
SW1 floods the ping into every VLAN until PC-B answers
It fails: PC-A sends to its default gateway, and nothing answers for that address
SW1 routes it, because switches route between their own VLANs by default
check.explanation: PC-B is in another subnet, so PC-A needs its gateway. With no Layer 3 device in VLAN 10, the ARP for the gateway goes unanswered. A Layer 2 switch never forwards frames between VLANs.

sections.title: Router on a stick: one trunk, many subinterfaces
sections.key: Router on a stick trunks one router port to the switch and gives each VLAN a subinterface with encapsulation dot1q and that VLAN's gateway address.
sections.body:
A branch has R1 and SW1 with VLANs 10 and 20. Instead of two router ports, you cable G0/0 to SW1 as an 802.1Q trunk and split it into **subinterfaces**:

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Each subinterface adds its own connected and local routes. The switch port must be a static trunk (`switchport mode trunk`, VLANs allowed), because routers do not speak DTP.

[[visual 2]]

Every routed packet crosses the trunk twice. That **hairpin** makes the single link a bottleneck as the site grows.

visual.title: Building a subinterface
rows: Creates the subinterface. The number is only a label; matching the VLAN ID is a convention
Handles frames tagged 10. IOS refuses an IP address until this is set
A subinterface is never more up than its parent; a shut parent takes them all down

sections.code:
R1(config)# interface g0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface g0/0.10
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1q 10
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# interface g0/0.20
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1q 20
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0

SW1(config)# interface g0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
sections.tip: On each subinterface: encapsulation first, IP address second. The parent interface needs no address, just no shutdown.
sections.pitfall: Forgetting no shutdown on the physical interface. The subinterfaces then show administratively down even though you never shut them.

activity.title: Build router-on-a-stick
activity.prompt: Bring up G0/0, then build G0/0.10 and G0/0.20. Enter encapsulation dot1q before the IP address on each subinterface. Finish with show ip interface brief and look for both subinterfaces up/up with their gateway addresses.

check.question: Which command on subinterface G0/0.30 tells the router to handle frames tagged with VLAN 30?
choices: encapsulation dot1q 30
switchport access vlan 30
switchport trunk allowed vlan 30
vlan 30
check.explanation: Router subinterfaces bind to a VLAN with encapsulation dot1q <vlan-id>. The switchport and vlan commands are switch commands; a router port is not a switchport.

sections.title: The native VLAN, and verifying router on a stick
sections.key: The router must treat the trunk's native VLAN as untagged too, and because each device sees only its own half, verify router on a stick on both.
sections.body:
The trunk sends its **native VLAN** untagged, so R1 must know which interface owns untagged frames. Two options:

[[visual]]

Either way, it must match the switch trunk's native VLAN. If the switch sends VLAN 99 untagged but R1 expects it tagged, that subnet breaks.

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

Each device sees only its own half. If the switch port is an access port, or VLAN 20 is not allowed, R1 still shows its subinterfaces up/up with connected routes. Check both ends.

visual.title: Serving the native VLAN on R1

items.title: Native subinterface
points: Sends VLAN 99 untagged and takes untagged frames as VLAN 99

visual.title: Verify both halves
rows: Each subinterface, its address and status (which follows the parent)
A C and an L route per working subinterface
Which subinterface handles each VLAN, with counters; the native one adds `Native-vlan Tx-type: Untagged`
Trunking, the native VLAN, and each VLAN allowed, active and forwarding

sections.code:
R1# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     unassigned      YES unset  up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/0.10  192.168.10.1    YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/0.20  192.168.20.1    YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/0.99  192.168.99.1    YES manual up                    up

R1# show running-config interface g0/0.99
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.99
 encapsulation dot1Q 99 native
 ip address 192.168.99.1 255.255.255.0

SW1# show interfaces trunk
Port        Mode         Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/1       on           802.1q         trunking      99

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/1       10,20,99
sections.tip: Verify ROAS from both sides: the router (show ip interface brief, show vlans) and the switch (show interfaces trunk).
sections.pitfall: Trusting the router's up/up subinterfaces as proof the design works. The router cannot see a misconfigured switch port.

check.question: R1's subinterfaces are up/up and show ip route lists both connected subnets, yet no host can reach its gateway. R1's configuration is correct. What should you check next?
choices: Whether R1 needs ip routing enabled for subinterfaces
Whether R1 needs OSPF to route between its subinterfaces
Whether R1's physical G0/0 needs its own IP address
The switch port facing R1: is it trunking, and are VLANs 10 and 20 allowed and active?
check.explanation: Routers do not negotiate trunks and cannot detect switch-side mistakes, so an access port or a pruned VLAN on SW1 breaks ROAS silently. Routers route between connected subnets without any routing protocol, and the physical interface needs an address only for the native VLAN option.

sections.title: Layer 3 switches and SVIs
sections.key: A Layer 3 switch routes between VLANs in hardware once ip routing is on, with one SVI per VLAN (interface vlan 10) as that VLAN's gateway.
sections.body:
A campus with 30 VLANs cannot push everything through one router trunk. A **Layer 3 switch** switches frames within each VLAN and routes between VLANs, in hardware, with no hairpin.

Each VLAN's gateway is a **switched virtual interface (SVI)**, created with `interface vlan 10`. It is not tied to a port: it is the switch's own presence in the VLAN, reachable through any port in it.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Without `ip routing`, the SVIs still answer pings from their own VLAN, but nothing is routed, and `show ip route` prints `Default gateway is not set` and an ICMP redirect cache instead of a routing table.

visual.title: Turn a switch into the gateway

steps.label: Routing template, if needed
steps.detail: `sdm prefer lanbase-routing` and reload, on models that reject `ip routing` as invalid input

steps.label: `ip routing`
steps.detail: Global config. Without it, SVIs are only management interfaces

steps.label: A way out
steps.detail: A default route or OSPF, if traffic leaves the campus

sections.code:
DSW1(config)# ip routing
DSW1(config)# vlan 10
DSW1(config-vlan)# vlan 20
DSW1(config-vlan)# exit
DSW1(config)# interface vlan 10
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# interface vlan 20
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# end
DSW1# show ip route connected
! legend and subnet headers omitted
C        192.168.10.0/24 is directly connected, Vlan10
L        192.168.10.1/32 is directly connected, Vlan10
C        192.168.20.0/24 is directly connected, Vlan20
L        192.168.20.1/32 is directly connected, Vlan20
sections.deeper: In a typical campus the access switches stay Layer 2. They trunk the user VLANs up to a pair of distribution Layer 3 switches, and the SVIs live there. Two switches serving the same VLAN raise a new question (which one is the gateway?), which first hop redundancy protocols such as HSRP answer in a later lesson. Routing protocols such as OSPF run on SVIs exactly as on router interfaces.
sections.tip: Hosts can ping their SVI gateway but nothing in another VLAN? Check for ip routing before anything else.
sections.pitfall: Forgetting ip routing. The SVIs come up and answer pings from their own VLAN, so everything looks healthy, but nothing is routed between VLANs.

activity.title: Turn a switch into the gateway
activity.prompt: In this free switch sandbox, PC1 on G0/1 is 10.0.10.11 and PC2 on G0/2 is 10.0.20.12. Enable ip routing, create VLANs 10 and 20, put G0/1 in VLAN 10 and G0/2 in VLAN 20, then build interface vlan 10 (10.0.10.1/24) and interface vlan 20 (10.0.20.1/24) with no shutdown. Check show ip route for the Vlan10 and Vlan20 connected routes and ping both PCs. Finally create interface vlan 30 with an address and explain why show ip interface brief lists it as up/down.

check.question: Which global command makes a Cisco Layer 3 switch route between its SVIs?
choices: ip default-gateway 192.168.10.1
ip routing
no switchport
ipv6 unicast-routing
check.explanation: ip routing enables IPv4 routing. ip default-gateway is what a switch uses when it is not routing, no switchport makes a physical port a routed port, and ipv6 unicast-routing enables IPv6 forwarding only.

sections.title: Following a packet through a Layer 3 switch
sections.key: A Layer 3 switch routes like a router: the host frames to the SVI's MAC, and the switch decrements the TTL and builds a new frame in the destination VLAN.
sections.body:
PC-A (192.168.10.11, VLAN 10) pings PC-B (192.168.20.22, VLAN 20). Their access switches trunk up to DSW1, which has SVIs 192.168.10.1 and 192.168.20.1.

[[visual]]

It is the same logic as router on a stick, but the packet never leaves the switch's hardware.

Traffic beyond the campus needs a routed uplink plus a default route or OSPF (with the user-VLAN SVIs passive). Then think about the **return path**: the WAN router needs routes back to the VLAN subnets, or inter-VLAN pings work while every reply from beyond is dropped.

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

messages.label: New frame in VLAN 20
messages.detail: src MAC DSW1, dst MAC PC-B

marks.text: Needs routes back to both VLANs

sections.code:
DSW1(config)# interface g1/0/24
DSW1(config-if)# no switchport
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.252
DSW1(config-if)# exit
DSW1(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.0.2

! The WAN router needs the way back to the VLAN subnets
WAN(config)# ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.1
WAN(config)# ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.1
sections.pitfall: Testing only between VLANs. Inter-VLAN pings can work while traffic to the WAN fails, because the upstream router has no route back to the VLAN subnets.

check.question: DSW1 routes a packet from PC-A (VLAN 10) to PC-B (VLAN 20). In the frame DSW1 sends out toward PC-B, what is the source MAC address?
choices: PC-A's MAC address, because switches never change MAC addresses
DSW1's own MAC address, because DSW1 routed the packet and built a new frame
The broadcast address, because DSW1 floods routed packets
PC-B's MAC address
check.explanation: Once DSW1 routes, it behaves like a router: it discards the incoming frame and builds a new one with its own MAC as the source and PC-B's MAC (learned with ARP in VLAN 20) as the destination. Source MACs are preserved only when a frame is switched within one VLAN.

sections.title: When an SVI stays down
sections.key: An SVI is up/up only when its VLAN exists, is not shut down, has at least one up and forwarding port, and the SVI itself is not shut down.
sections.body:
You create `interface vlan 20` with an address and `no shutdown`, yet it shows up/down. The SVI is fine; its VLAN is not.

[[visual]]

Two statuses to read quickly:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

In the exhibit, Vlan20 is up/down because no port carries VLAN 20, and Vlan30 is administratively down. The VLAN and the VLAN interface are separate objects with separate `shutdown` commands, and both must be enabled.

visual.title: Four conditions for up/up
rows: Deleting it (`no vlan 20`), or never creating it
The VLAN is not shut down
`shutdown` under `vlan 20`: show vlan brief says act/lshut
An up port carries the VLAN
No up/up access port in it, and no trunk that allows it, has it active and is STP forwarding
The SVI is not shut down

items.title: up / down
points: The SVI is enabled, but its VLAN is missing, shut down or has no active port
Look at `show vlan brief` and `show interfaces trunk`

sections.code:
DSW1# show ip interface brief | include Vlan
Vlan1                  unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
Vlan10                 192.168.10.1    YES manual up                    up
Vlan20                 192.168.20.1    YES manual up                    down
Vlan30                 192.168.30.1    YES manual administratively down down

DSW1# show vlan brief
VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------
1    default                          active    Gi1/0/3, Gi1/0/4, Gi1/0/5
10   SALES                            active    Gi1/0/1, Gi1/0/2
20   ENG                              active
30   VOICE                            active    Gi1/0/6
sections.tip: SVI up/down means look at the VLAN: does it exist, does any up port carry it, is the VLAN shut down?
sections.pitfall: Typing no shutdown on the SVI over and over when the real problem is a VLAN with no active ports. An SVI can be enabled and still down.

check.question: Vlan20 shows up/down. VLAN 20 exists and the SVI has no shutdown. What is the most likely cause?
choices: ip routing is disabled
No up/up access port or forwarding trunk carries VLAN 20 on this switch
The SVI has the wrong IP address
The switch has no default route
check.explanation: An enabled SVI goes up/down when its VLAN has no active ports. ip routing, the address and routes affect forwarding, not the SVI's line protocol.

sections.title: Routed ports: no switchport
sections.key: no switchport makes a Layer 3 switch port a routed port: no VLAN, no STP, an IP address on the port itself; ideal for one link between Layer 3 devices.
sections.body:
DSW1 has one uplink to the WAN router: one subnet, two devices. Instead of a VLAN plus an SVI, make the port a **routed port** with `no switchport`.

A routed port belongs to no VLAN, learns no MACs, runs no STP and takes an IP address like a router interface. Until you enter `no switchport`, IOS refuses the address: `% IP addresses may not be configured on L2 links.`

It is one interface in one subnet, so it cannot serve a VLAN spread over many ports; that needs an SVI.

[[code]]

[[visual]]

visual.title: How a routed port shows up
rows: The physical interface as the exit of its connected route
The IP address, as on a router

sections.code:
DSW1(config)# interface g1/0/24
DSW1(config-if)# no switchport
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.252
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# end
DSW1# show interfaces status | include Gi1/0/24
Gi1/0/24                     connected    routed       a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
DSW1# show interfaces g1/0/24 switchport
Name: Gi1/0/24
Switchport: Disabled
DSW1# show ip route connected | include 1/0/24
C        10.0.0.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet1/0/24
L        10.0.0.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet1/0/24
sections.tip: SVI for a VLAN with many ports; routed port for a link with exactly two devices, such as distribution to core or a switch to a WAN router or firewall.
sections.pitfall: Typing ip address on a port that is still a switchport and getting "% IP addresses may not be configured on L2 links." Enter no switchport first.

check.question: Which link is the best fit for a routed port instead of an SVI?
choices: A user VLAN with 40 access ports
A trunk carrying VLANs 10, 20 and 30 to another switch
A voice VLAN shared by phones on every floor
A single point-to-point uplink from a Layer 3 switch to a WAN router
check.explanation: A routed port is one physical link in one subnet with no VLAN, perfect for an uplink between two Layer 3 devices. Subnets spread across many ports or carried on trunks need SVIs.

sections.title: Layer 3 EtherChannel, and choosing a design
sections.key: Parallel links between Layer 3 devices become one Layer 3 EtherChannel: no switchport on every member, and the single IP address on interface port-channel.
sections.body:
Distribution and core switches usually share two or more links. As separate routed ports, each link brings its own OSPF neighbor and route. A **Layer 3 EtherChannel** makes them one routed interface: one subnet, one neighbor, with traffic balanced across the members.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

In `show etherchannel summary`, **R** means Layer 3 and **S** Layer 2: `Po1(RU)` is a routed bundle in use, with members marked (P). A bundle meant to route that shows `Po1(SU)` is missing `no switchport`.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Building it
rows: `no switchport` and `channel-group 1 mode active` (LACP; `mode on` is static). The group number is local and may differ on the neighbor
`no switchport` (IOS often adds it) and the one IP address; members carry none
Routed, same speed and same duplex, or they do not bundle

visual.title: Choosing a design
rows: Many ports share a subnet (user VLANs)
One link between two Layer 3 devices
Parallel links between two Layer 3 devices
Small site with a router and a Layer 2 switch

sections.code:
DSW1(config)# interface range gigabitethernet1/0/1 - 2
DSW1(config-if-range)# no switchport
DSW1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
DSW1(config-if-range)# exit
DSW1(config)# interface port-channel 1
DSW1(config-if)# no switchport
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.1.1 255.255.255.252
DSW1(config-if)# end
DSW1# show etherchannel summary
Flags:  D - down        P - bundled in port-channel
        R - Layer3      S - Layer2
        U - in use      f - failed to allocate aggregator
! lines omitted
Group  Port-channel  Protocol    Ports
------+-------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------
1      Po1(RU)         LACP      Gi1/0/1(P)  Gi1/0/2(P)
sections.pitfall: Putting IP addresses on the member ports. The bundle is one routed interface, so the single address belongs on interface port-channel.

check.question: Which link is the best fit for a Layer 3 EtherChannel?
choices: A user VLAN with 40 access ports
A single uplink from a Layer 3 switch to a WAN router
A trunk carrying VLANs 10, 20 and 30 to an access switch
Two parallel links between a distribution switch and a core switch that both route
check.explanation: Parallel links between two Layer 3 devices become one routed bundle with one subnet and one routing neighbor. A single link only needs a routed port, user VLANs need SVIs, and a trunk to an access switch stays Layer 2.

sections.title: Troubleshooting inter-VLAN routing
sections.key: When one VLAN cannot route, work outward from the host: its gateway, its access port, the trunk, then the subinterface's dot1q tag or the SVI and ip routing.
sections.body:
Ticket: "VLAN 20 cannot reach anything outside VLAN 20; VLAN 10 is fine." Work outward, one layer at a time:

[[visual]]

[[code]]

The exhibit shows the sneakiest ROAS fault. G0/0.20 is up/up with the right address, but its encapsulation is VLAN 200. Frames tagged 20 match no subinterface, and replies leave tagged 200. `show vlans` gives it away.

Prove any fix from a VLAN 20 host: ping its gateway (access port, trunk and tag), then a VLAN 10 host (routing and the return path).

steps.label: Host
steps.detail: Right IP and mask, and the gateway is its own VLAN's address (192.168.20.1), inside its own subnet

steps.label: Access switch
steps.detail: The port is an access port in VLAN 20: `show vlan brief`

steps.label: Trunk
steps.detail: Trunking, VLAN 20 allowed, active and forwarding, native VLAN matches: `show interfaces trunk`

steps.label: Router on a stick
steps.detail: `encapsulation dot1q 20` on the right subinterface, right address, parent not shut

steps.label: Layer 3 switch
steps.detail: `ip routing` is on (else: Default gateway is not set), and Vlan20 is up/up

sections.code:
R1# show running-config | section GigabitEthernet0/0.20
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 200
 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0

R1# show vlans
! output trimmed to the VLAN 20 gateway
Virtual LAN ID:  200 (IEEE 802.1Q Encapsulation)
   vLAN Trunk Interface:   GigabitEthernet0/0.20
   Protocols Configured:   Address:          Received:        Transmitted:
           IP              192.168.20.1              0                 12

DSW2# show ip route
Default gateway is not set

Host               Gateway           Last Use    Total Uses  Interface
ICMP redirect cache is empty
sections.tip: Up/up proves the interface is enabled, not that its VLAN tag is right. Read the encapsulation line.
sections.pitfall: Retyping the IP address on a subinterface that already has the right one. When one VLAN fails and the rest work, compare that VLAN's encapsulation number first.

activity.title: Troubleshoot: one VLAN cannot route
activity.prompt: VLAN 20 hosts cannot reach 192.168.20.1 while VLAN 10 works. Use show running-config and show ip interface brief to find the fault, then fix G0/0.20 without touching G0/0.10. Notice how healthy the broken subinterface looks in show ip interface brief.

check.question: A Layer 3 switch has SVIs up/up for VLANs 10 and 20. Hosts ping their own gateway but not hosts in the other VLAN, and show ip route prints "Default gateway is not set". What is the fix?
choices: Configure ip routing in global configuration mode
Configure no shutdown on both SVIs
Add a default route to the switch
Configure no switchport on the SVIs
check.explanation: That show ip route output appears when IP routing is disabled. The SVIs are already up/up, a default route would not enable routing, and no switchport applies to physical ports, not SVIs.

keyTerms.definition: Routing packets between the subnets of different VLANs using a Layer 3 device that has an interface in each.
One router interface on an 802.1Q trunk, with one subinterface per VLAN acting as its gateway.
A logical interface such as G0/0.10 that carves a physical router interface into several Layer 3 interfaces.
The subinterface command that binds it to one 802.1Q VLAN ID (add native for the untagged VLAN).
The VLAN a trunk carries untagged; router and switch must agree on it.
A switch that also routes IP packets between VLANs in hardware once ip routing is enabled.
Switched virtual interface (interface vlan N): a Layer 3 switch's routed interface into a VLAN, used as its gateway.
A Layer 3 switch port with no switchport: no VLAN, an IP address directly on the port.
Global command that enables IPv4 routing on a Layer 3 switch.
Router-on-a-stick traffic pattern: a routed packet crosses the same trunk twice, up in one VLAN and down in another.
A switch memory profile; some models need a routing template (sdm prefer) and a reload before ip routing is accepted.
Parallel routed links bundled into one routed interface, with the IP address on interface port-channel.

summary: Each VLAN is its own subnet, so its hosts need a gateway on a subinterface, an SVI or a routed interface.
ROAS: no shutdown on the parent, encapsulation dot1q before the IP address on each subinterface, and a static trunk on the switch.
Layer 3 switch: ip routing, the VLANs, and interface vlan N with an address; upstream routers need routes back.
An SVI is up/up only if its VLAN exists, is not shut, has an active port, and the SVI is not shut.
Routed ports (no switchport) suit single links between Layer 3 devices; parallel links become a Layer 3 EtherChannel.
A wrong dot1q tag still shows up/up, so read the configuration and check both router and switch.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new technician how a ping from a PC in VLAN 10 reaches a PC in VLAN 20, first through router-on-a-stick and then through a Layer 3 switch, and why a typo in one encapsulation dot1q command breaks only one VLAN.

questions.question: Why can't a Layer 2 switch forward traffic between VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 on its own?
choices: VLAN tags make frames too large to switch
The switch has no MAC addresses for hosts in other VLANs' ports
Each VLAN is a separate broadcast domain and subnet, and a Layer 2 switch forwards frames only within a VLAN
Spanning tree blocks all ports between VLANs
questions.explanation: VLANs deliberately split a switch into separate Layer 2 domains, each with its own subnet. Moving traffic between them is routing, which needs a Layer 3 device acting as each VLAN's gateway. STP has nothing to do with VLAN separation.

questions.question: PC-A (192.168.10.11/24, gateway 192.168.10.1) sends a packet to PC-B at 192.168.20.22. Which destination MAC address does PC-A use?
choices: PC-B's MAC address
The broadcast MAC address
The MAC address of the switch port PC-B is connected to
The MAC address of whichever device owns 192.168.10.1 (a router subinterface or SVI)
questions.explanation: The destination is in another subnet, so PC-A frames the packet to its gateway. With ROAS that is R1's G0/0 MAC; with a Layer 3 switch it is the SVI's MAC. PC-A never ARPs for a host in another subnet.

questions.question: Match each inter-VLAN routing design to its description.

pairs.right: One physical router port and access link for each VLAN
A VLAN interface on a Layer 3 switch acting as the VLAN's gateway
A Layer 3 switch port configured with no switchport and an IP address

questions.explanation: All four give each subnet a gateway. They differ in where that gateway lives and how well they scale: per-VLAN router ports waste ports, ROAS funnels everything through one trunk, and SVIs and routed ports route in switch hardware.

questions.question: You are in configuration mode for subinterface G0/0.10. Type the command that associates it with VLAN 10.
questions.explanation: encapsulation dot1q <vlan-id> binds a router subinterface to an 802.1Q VLAN. The subinterface number (.10) is only a label and does not set the VLAN.

questions.question: PC-A (VLAN 10) sends a packet to PC-B (VLAN 20) through router-on-a-stick. Put the steps in order.
items: PC-A sends a frame to its gateway's MAC; SW1 receives it on an access port in VLAN 10
SW1 forwards the frame over the trunk to R1, tagged VLAN 10
R1 receives it on G0/0.10 and routes the packet out G0/0.20
R1 sends a new frame back over the same trunk, tagged VLAN 20
SW1 removes the tag and delivers the frame out PC-B's access port in VLAN 20
questions.explanation: The packet goes up the trunk in VLAN 10 and comes back down in VLAN 20. That double trip across one link is the ROAS hairpin.

questions.question: An engineer creates G0/0.30 and types the ip address command first. IOS refuses it. Why?
choices: Subinterfaces cannot have IP addresses; only the physical interface can
IOS requires an encapsulation dot1q command on a LAN subinterface before it accepts an IP address
The physical interface must have an IP address first
The subinterface number must match a VLAN that exists on the router
questions.explanation: Until the subinterface knows its VLAN, IOS will not let it route. Set encapsulation dot1q 30, then the ip address. Routers do not have a VLAN database, and the physical interface needs no address.

questions.question: What is the main performance drawback of router-on-a-stick compared with a Layer 3 switch?
choices: The router must run a routing protocol between its subinterfaces
Each subinterface needs its own physical cable
All inter-VLAN traffic crosses the single trunk twice, so that one link can become a bottleneck
Hosts must use the router's physical interface address as their gateway
questions.explanation: Routed traffic goes up the trunk in the source VLAN and back down in the destination VLAN. A Layer 3 switch routes internally in hardware. Connected subinterfaces need no routing protocol, and each VLAN uses its own subinterface address as the gateway.

questions.question: Hosts in VLANs 10 and 20 cannot reach their gateways. What is wrong with R1's configuration?
questions.code:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 no ip address
 shutdown
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 20
 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
choices: The physical G0/0 is shut down, which takes every subinterface down with it
G0/0 needs an IP address before subinterfaces can work
The subinterfaces need no shutdown commands of their own
dot1Q must be lowercase for the encapsulation to apply
questions.explanation: A subinterface's status can never be better than its parent's, so the shutdown on G0/0 leaves both subinterfaces administratively down. The physical interface needs only no shutdown; an address is optional (used for the native VLAN). IOS commands are not case sensitive.

questions.question: Which configuration does the switch port connected to R1's router-on-a-stick interface need?
choices: switchport mode trunk, with the router's VLANs allowed
switchport mode dynamic auto, so the router can negotiate the trunk
switchport mode access with switchport access vlan 10
no switchport with an IP address in each VLAN
questions.explanation: The link must carry several VLANs, so it must be a trunk. Routers do not speak DTP, so dynamic auto would stay an access port. An access port would carry only one VLAN.

questions.question: You are configuring subinterface G0/0.99 for VLAN 99, which is the trunk's native VLAN. Type the encapsulation command.
questions.explanation: The native keyword tells R1 that VLAN 99 travels untagged on this trunk, so untagged frames belong to G0/0.99 and frames sent from it go out untagged.

questions.question: Besides a subinterface with the native keyword, how else can a router-on-a-stick router serve the native VLAN's subnet?
choices: Configure the native VLAN as a separate SVI
Add switchport trunk native vlan to the router interface
Configure the IP address on the physical interface, with no encapsulation command
It cannot; the native VLAN is never routed
questions.explanation: Untagged frames are handled by the physical interface, so its IP address becomes the native VLAN's gateway. SVIs and switchport commands belong to switches, and the native VLAN can certainly be routed.

questions.question: SW1's trunk to R1 uses native VLAN 99, so VLAN 99 frames arrive at R1 untagged. VLAN 10 works, but hosts in VLAN 99 cannot reach 192.168.99.1. Which change fixes it?
questions.code:
R1# show running-config | section GigabitEthernet0/0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 no ip address
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.99
 encapsulation dot1Q 99
 ip address 192.168.99.1 255.255.255.0
choices: Change G0/0.99 to encapsulation dot1q 1
Change G0/0.99 to encapsulation dot1q 99 native
Change the switch's trunk to switchport mode access
questions.explanation: R1 expects VLAN 99 frames to be tagged, but the switch sends them untagged, so they land on the physical interface instead of G0/0.99. Adding native to the subinterface (or moving the address to the physical interface) aligns R1 with the switch. An access port would break VLAN 10.

questions.question: Type the router command that lists each 802.1Q VLAN, the subinterface handling it, and which one is native.
questions.explanation: On a router, show vlans maps VLAN IDs to subinterfaces and marks the native VLAN. On a switch, the equivalent views are show vlan brief and show interfaces trunk.

questions.question: VLAN 10 hosts reach their gateway on R1, but VLAN 20 hosts do not. R1's G0/0.20 is correct. Based on SW1's output, what is the fix?
questions.code:
SW1# show interfaces trunk
Port        Mode         Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/1       on           802.1q         trunking      1

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/1       10

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi0/1       10

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
Gi0/1       10
choices: Change the native VLAN to 20
Configure ip routing on SW1
Create subinterface G0/0.20 on SW1
Add VLAN 20 to the trunk's allowed list on SW1
questions.explanation: Only VLAN 10 is allowed on Gi0/1, so VLAN 20 frames never cross the trunk to R1. The router has no way to notice. switchport trunk allowed vlan add 20 fixes it without removing VLAN 10.

questions.question: Type the switch interface command that adds VLAN 20 to a trunk's existing allowed list without removing the VLANs already allowed.
questions.explanation: The add keyword appends to the list. Typing switchport trunk allowed vlan 20 would replace the whole list with only VLAN 20, cutting off VLAN 10.

questions.question: Type the global command that enables IPv4 routing on a Cisco Layer 3 switch.
questions.explanation: With ip routing enabled, the switch routes between its SVIs and routed ports. Some models also need a routing SDM template (sdm prefer) and a reload first.

questions.question: In an SVI design, what default gateway should hosts in VLAN 10 use?
choices: The management IP address of the access switch
The IP address of the switch's uplink routed port
The IP address of interface Vlan10 on the Layer 3 switch
Any address in the subnet, as long as the switch routes
questions.explanation: Each SVI is its VLAN's gateway. The routed uplink belongs to a different subnet, and a host's gateway must be the exact address of a Layer 3 interface in its own subnet.

questions.question: Complete the configuration so the switch becomes the gateway for VLAN 30.
questions.code:
DSW1(config)# ip routing
DSW1(config)# _____
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.30.1 255.255.255.0
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
choices: interface vlan 30
vlan 30
switchport access vlan 30
interface g1/0/30
questions.explanation: interface vlan 30 creates the SVI and enters interface mode (config-if). vlan 30 creates the VLAN itself in config-vlan mode, switchport access vlan is a port command, and a physical port would need no switchport before taking an address.

questions.question: On a Layer 3 switch, show ip route prints only the lines below. What does it tell you?
questions.code:
DSW1# show ip route
Default gateway is not set

Host               Gateway           Last Use    Total Uses  Interface
ICMP redirect cache is empty
choices: The switch is routing but has no default route
All SVIs are down
The routing table is empty because no routing protocol runs
IP routing is disabled, so the switch is acting as a host rather than routing between VLANs
questions.explanation: When ip routing is off, IOS shows the default gateway and ICMP redirect cache instead of a routing table. A routing switch with no default route would still list "Gateway of last resort is not set" and its connected routes.

questions.question: Which two are advantages of routing with SVIs on a Layer 3 switch instead of router-on-a-stick? Choose two.
choices: Hosts no longer need a default gateway
Routing happens in switch hardware without sending traffic over a trunk twice
VLANs no longer need to be created
It scales to many VLANs without one link becoming a bottleneck
ip routing is not required
questions.explanation: SVIs route inside the switch, so there is no hairpin and no single router link to saturate. Hosts still need a gateway (the SVI), VLANs must exist for SVIs to come up, and ip routing must be enabled.

questions.question: Users in VLAN 30 have no gateway. Based on the output, what is the fix?
questions.code:
DSW1# show ip interface brief | include Vlan30
Vlan30                 192.168.30.1    YES manual administratively down down

DSW1# show vlan brief | include ^30
30   VOICE                            active    Gi1/0/6
choices: Create VLAN 30 with the vlan 30 command
Enter interface vlan 30 and configure no shutdown
Configure ip routing
Assign an IP address to Vlan30
questions.explanation: "administratively down" means the SVI itself is shut. VLAN 30 exists and has a port (Gi1/0/6), and the address is already configured.

questions.question: Which three conditions are required for SVI Vlan20 to be up/up? Choose three.
choices: The switch has a default route
VLAN 20 exists on the switch
A host in VLAN 20 has sent traffic to the SVI
At least one up/up access port in VLAN 20, or a forwarding trunk that carries it
ip routing is enabled
Interface vlan 20 is not shut down
questions.explanation: The SVI's status follows its VLAN: the VLAN must exist, be carried by an active port and not be shut, and the SVI must be enabled. Routes and ip routing affect forwarding, not interface status, and no host traffic is needed.

questions.question: Interface vlan 40 has an address and no shutdown, and Gi1/0/9 was an access port in VLAN 40 until someone ran cleanup commands this morning. Based on the output, why is Vlan40 up/down?
questions.code:
DSW1# show ip interface brief | include Vlan40
Vlan40                 192.168.40.1    YES manual up                    down

DSW1# show vlan brief
VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------
1    default                          active    Gi1/0/3, Gi1/0/4, Gi1/0/5
10   SALES                            active    Gi1/0/1, Gi1/0/2
20   ENG                              active    Gi1/0/7
choices: VLAN 40 does not exist in the switch's VLAN database
The SVI is administratively down
ip routing is disabled
Gi1/0/9 is a routed port
questions.explanation: show vlan brief has no VLAN 40: it was deleted, so Gi1/0/9 (still assigned to VLAN 40) is inactive and the SVI has no VLAN to attach to. Recreating it with vlan 40 reactivates Gi1/0/9 and brings the SVI up. The SVI is not administratively down, and ip routing does not affect interface status.

questions.question: Type the interface command that turns a Layer 3 switch port into a routed port.
questions.explanation: no switchport removes Layer 2 behavior from the port so it acts like a router interface and accepts an IP address directly.

questions.question: In show interfaces status on a Layer 3 switch, what appears in the VLAN column for a routed port?
choices: trunk
routed
unassigned
questions.explanation: A routed port belongs to no VLAN, so IOS shows "routed" instead of an access VLAN number or "trunk".

questions.question: The engineer wants Gi1/0/24 to be a routed uplink. Why was the command rejected?
questions.code:
DSW1(config)# interface g1/0/24
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.252
% IP addresses may not be configured on L2 links.
choices: A /30 mask is not allowed on switch ports
ip routing must be configured inside the interface first
The interface must be shut down before addressing it
The port is still a Layer 2 switchport; it needs no switchport before it accepts an IP address
questions.explanation: Switch ports default to switchport (Layer 2) mode, and IOS refuses an IP address on a Layer 2 port. no switchport converts it to a routed port that accepts the address. ip routing is a global command, and /30 masks are fine.

questions.question: You bundle Gi1/0/1 and Gi1/0/2 into a Layer 3 EtherChannel to a router. Where does the IP address go?
choices: On each member interface, with the same address on both
On interface port-channel 1, with no switchport on the port-channel and its member ports
On an SVI for the VLAN the members belong to
On Gi1/0/1 only, since the first member carries all routed traffic
questions.explanation: A Layer 3 EtherChannel is one routed link: the members and the port-channel are routed (no switchport) and the address lives on the port-channel interface. Members do not get their own addresses, and there is no VLAN or SVI involved.

questions.question: VLAN 20 hosts cannot reach 192.168.20.1, while VLAN 10 works. What is the fix?
questions.code:
R1# show running-config | section GigabitEthernet0/0.20
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 200
 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0

R1# show ip interface brief | include 0/0.20
GigabitEthernet0/0.20  192.168.20.1    YES manual up                    up
choices: Under G0/0.20, configure no shutdown
Change the subinterface number from .20 to .200
Under G0/0.20, configure encapsulation dot1q 20
Configure ip routing on R1
questions.explanation: The subinterface is tagged for VLAN 200, so frames from VLAN 20 never match it. Its status is up/up and the number after the dot does not set the VLAN. Routers route between connected interfaces without an ip routing command (it is on by default).

questions.question: PC-B (192.168.20.22/24) can ping other VLAN 20 hosts but nothing outside VLAN 20. Routing is configured correctly for both VLANs. PC-B's gateway is set to 192.168.10.1. What is wrong?
choices: PC-B's gateway is not in its own subnet, so PC-B can never reach it; it should be 192.168.20.1
PC-B needs to be moved to VLAN 10 to reach its gateway
The router must answer ARP for 192.168.10.1 in VLAN 20
PC-B needs a /16 mask so 192.168.10.1 is local
questions.explanation: A host only ARPs for addresses in its own subnet, so a gateway in another subnet is unusable. Fix the host, not the network: VLAN 20's gateway is 192.168.20.1. Changing VLANs or masks would break the addressing plan.

questions.question: Name four common reasons one VLAN cannot route while the others work.
questions.answer: Any four of: wrong encapsulation dot1q VLAN on the subinterface; VLAN not allowed or not active on the trunk; native VLAN mismatch between router and switch; host gateway or mask wrong; access port in the wrong VLAN; SVI down because the VLAN is missing, has no active ports or is shut down; SVI shut down.
questions.explanation: When only one VLAN fails, the problem is almost always specific to that VLAN: its tag, its place on the trunk, its SVI, or its hosts. A global setting like ip routing would break every VLAN at once.

questions.question: What does this part of R1's show vlans output tell you?
questions.code:
R1# show vlans
! output trimmed
Virtual LAN ID:  99 (IEEE 802.1Q Encapsulation)

   vLAN Trunk Interface:   GigabitEthernet0/0.99

 This is configured as native Vlan for the following interface(s) :
GigabitEthernet0/0
   Native-vlan Tx-type: Untagged

   Protocols Configured:   Address:              Received:        Transmitted:
           IP              192.168.99.1                  3                 4
choices: G0/0.99 is configured with encapsulation dot1q 99 native, so VLAN 99 travels untagged on the trunk
VLAN 99 is not allowed on the trunk
G0/0.99 tags every frame it sends with VLAN 99
The physical interface G0/0 owns 192.168.99.1
questions.explanation: The native lines appear when a subinterface uses the native keyword: R1 sends VLAN 99 untagged and treats untagged frames as VLAN 99. The address belongs to G0/0.99, and the counters show traffic in both directions.

questions.question: PC-A (VLAN 10) pings PC-B (VLAN 20) through Layer 3 switch DSW1. Compared with the packet PC-A sent, what is different about the packet DSW1 forwards into VLAN 20?
choices: The destination IP address is changed to the Vlan20 SVI
Nothing; a switch forwards the packet unchanged
The source IP address becomes 192.168.20.1
The TTL is one lower, and the packet sits in a new frame with DSW1's MAC as the source
questions.explanation: Routing on an SVI is real routing: DSW1 decrements the TTL and re-encapsulates the packet in a new frame for VLAN 20. The IP addresses stay end to end (no NAT is involved).

questions.question: Hosts in VLANs 10 and 20 reach each other through DSW1, and DSW1 can ping the WAN router at 10.0.0.2. Yet no host can reach any server beyond the WAN router. DSW1 has `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.0.2`. What is the most likely cause?
choices: DSW1 needs ip routing enabled on each SVI
The WAN router has no route back to 192.168.10.0/24 and 192.168.20.0/24
The SVIs must be made passive
The hosts need the WAN router as their default gateway
questions.explanation: Requests leave through DSW1's default route, but replies from beyond must be routed back to the VLAN subnets. Without static routes or OSPF toward DSW1 on the WAN router, the replies are dropped. Inter-VLAN traffic works because DSW1 knows both subnets as connected routes.

questions.question: You are configuring a routed member port of a Layer 3 EtherChannel. Type the interface command that adds it to channel group 1 using LACP active negotiation.
questions.explanation: channel-group works the same for Layer 2 and Layer 3 bundles; mode active starts LACP negotiation, while mode on builds a static bundle. The member also needs no switchport, and the IP address goes on interface port-channel 1.

questions.question: The engineer wanted a routed link between DSW1 and the core, but the output below appears and ip address is rejected on Port-channel1. What is wrong?
questions.code:
DSW1# show etherchannel summary
! flags: R - Layer3, S - Layer2, U - in use, P - bundled in port-channel
Group  Port-channel  Protocol    Ports
------+-------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------
1      Po1(SU)         LACP      Gi1/0/1(P)  Gi1/0/2(P)
choices: LACP cannot build Layer 3 bundles; the mode must be on
The members are bundled but not up, so the address is refused
The bundle is Layer 2 (S); the members and the port-channel need no switchport before the address is accepted
The channel-group number must match the core switch's number
questions.explanation: S marks a Layer 2 EtherChannel, which cannot hold an IP address. With no switchport on the member ports and on Port-channel1 the bundle becomes Layer 3 (R). LACP works for both kinds of bundle, U and P show it is in use and bundled, and channel-group numbers are local to each switch.

questions.question: Interface vlan 20 has an address and no shutdown, and Gi1/0/7 is an up access port in VLAN 20, yet Vlan20 is up/down. Based on the output, why?
questions.code:
DSW1# show vlan brief
VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------
1    default                          active    Gi1/0/3, Gi1/0/4
10   SALES                            active    Gi1/0/1, Gi1/0/2
20   ENG                              act/lshut Gi1/0/7
choices: VLAN 20 itself has been shut down, and an SVI goes down when its VLAN is shut
Interface vlan 20 is administratively down
ip routing is disabled
Gi1/0/7 must be a trunk for the SVI to come up
questions.explanation: act/lshut means VLAN 20 was shut down locally (shutdown in VLAN configuration mode). The VLAN and the VLAN interface are separate objects with separate shutdown commands, and both must be enabled. An administratively down SVI would show "administratively down".

questions.question: DSW1 routes for VLAN 10 (192.168.10.1) and VLAN 20 (192.168.20.1). PC-B in VLAN 20 can ping 192.168.20.1 but cannot ping PC-A at 192.168.10.11. PC-A can ping 192.168.10.1, and its settings are below. What is wrong?
choices: PC-A's mask should be 255.255.0.0 so it can reach VLAN 20 directly
DSW1 needs a static route to 192.168.10.0/24
PC-B's request never reaches PC-A, because VLAN 10 is not allowed on the trunk
PC-A's replies go to 192.168.10.254, an address nobody owns; its gateway must be 192.168.10.1
questions.explanation: The request reaches PC-A, but PC-A sends replies for another subnet to its configured gateway, 192.168.10.254, which no device answers. Pinging 192.168.10.1 directly works because that is on-subnet and needs no gateway. DSW1 already has a connected route to 192.168.10.0/24.

questions.question: In `show etherchannel summary`, a bundle is listed as `Po1(RU)`. What does the R mean?
choices: The bundle uses RSTP
The bundle is a Layer 3 (routed) EtherChannel
The bundle is redundant and on standby
The bundle is in the process of resetting
questions.explanation: R marks a Layer 3 port-channel and S a Layer 2 one; U means the channel is in use. Member ports show (P) when they are bundled.

questions.question: R1 has `interface g0/0.100` configured with `encapsulation dot1q 30` and `ip address 10.30.0.1 255.255.255.0`. Which hosts use this subinterface as their gateway?
choices: Hosts in VLAN 100
Hosts in VLAN 30
Hosts in both VLAN 30 and VLAN 100
None, because the subinterface number must match the VLAN
questions.explanation: encapsulation dot1q sets the VLAN; the number after the dot is only a label. Matching them is a good habit, but a mismatch is legal and the subinterface still serves VLAN 30.

questions.question: Which three must be true for two ports to join the same Layer 3 EtherChannel on DSW1? Choose three.
choices: Both member ports are configured with no switchport
Each member port has its own IP address in the same subnet
The member ports use the same speed
The member ports use the same duplex
The channel-group number matches the one used on the neighboring switch
questions.explanation: Layer 3 bundles need routed members with matching speed and duplex. The address goes only on the port-channel interface, and channel-group numbers are local, so the neighbor may use a different number.
